p: Nadia Brooks spent five years as a test engineer at an avionics shop in Colorado Springs.
Now she's starting her first job as a systems engineer at Front Range Orbital, a space company that moved into an old lighting factory in Centennial.
Her father, Frank, was a lineman in Pueblo until the year she was nine.
Her sister Callie and her niece Rosie are two hours south in Pueblo.
FRO has only ever built cargo modules. Its next one is the first with people living inside.
The people you'll hear from first.
Amara Osei. Program manager. Ex Air Force, and she minds cost and schedule.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He's built pressure vessels for decades, and he hates paperwork.
Colleen Whitcomb. Nadia's mentor, a retired Air Force pilot.
Jun Takeda. Junior systems engineer. He keeps the SysML model.
Tiago Ferreira. Integration and test lead. He runs the high bay.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo Orbital's director of crew operations, once a flight surgeon.

Nadia Brooks found the note at ten to six, when she went looking for coffee in an apartment that still smelled like cardboard. Her sister Callie had driven up from Pueblo on Saturday in a borrowed truck with Rosie buckled in the back, carried boxes for six hours, and left before dark, because the drive home was close to two hours now. It used to be one.

Sticky note on the coffee maker. Coffee's in the cabinet left of the sink. Rosie's rocket is on the fridge. She says yours needs a bathroom and a window. I've got Dad. Call him Friday anyway. He says he isn't counting. He's counting. Don't get so busy up there you forget the way down here. Cal

The rocket was purple, with four stick people in the window, because Nadia had told Rosie on Saturday it was for four astronauts. Rosie had asked where they'd sleep. Nadia hadn't known. She stood in the kitchen looking at it longer than she meant to, then made the coffee.
At 6:40 she sat in her car in the Front Range Orbital lot and watched the sun come up behind a sign that still said Centennial Lighting Works.

The company had bought the old factory two years ago and never taken the sign down. Somebody had added a sticker under it, a little drawing of a space station, and that was the rebrand. Inside, she'd been told, was a high bay big enough to stand a city bus on its end, a pressure test cell, and four hundred people who built things that held air.

Her badge said Systems Engineer. She had never been one. For five years she had been a test engineer at an avionics shop in Colorado Springs, the person who wrote the procedure, ran the unit through it, and signed the sheet that said it passed. She was good at it. She was fast and careful and she never fudged a number.

She knew exactly why she'd picked that work. Her father had climbed poles for Xcel until the year he stopped, the year she was nine, and nobody in the house talked about that year. What she took from it was simple. A check that passed was the only thing that let anybody sleep.
Her phone buzzed. Dad, thirty one years on the lines, and these days he texted only in capital letters.
A text from Dad. FIRST DAY. PROUD OF YOU. REMEMBER YOU DONT CLIMB A POLE YOU HAVENT GROUNDED.
She smiled, typed back a heart, and went inside.

By nine she was in a conference room with a whiteboard that still had a lighting fixture wiring diagram ghosted under the erasures. At the head of the table sat Wes Harland, the chief engineer, fifty eight, sleeves rolled, the man who had designed more pressure vessels than anyone in the building. Amara Osei, the program manager, had the signed contract open on her laptop. Tiago Ferreira from integration and test leaned against the wall with a coffee. A young engineer named Jun Takeda had a laptop covered in stickers and an open modeling tool.

Halo Orbital signed Friday, Amara said. HEARTH. A habitat module for their station. Ninety cubic meters, crew of four, fifteen year design life, launch in thirty months. Firm fixed price on development. This is the biggest thing this company has ever won, and the people who will sleep in it are astronauts.
It's a can with air in it, Wes said. We've built eleven cargo modules. We know what to build. I'd like a layout on this board by Friday.
Everyone looked at the new systems engineer. Nadia thought about her father, and about how sure that crew had been.
Colleen's Flight Notes: start with the problem.
What a systems engineer is for.

Colleen Whitcomb met her at a diner on Arapahoe Road that afternoon and ordered pie for both of them. Nadia had met her four years ago, when Colleen was the Air Force pilot flying the evaluation flights on the displays Nadia's shop tested. After one debrief Nadia had stayed behind and asked her what the cold start test was actually for. Colleen had looked at her for a long second and then told her. She'd retired since, joined FRO's advisory board, and put Nadia's name in front of Wes.

Nadia told her about Wes and the can with air in it. Colleen listened without interrupting. Then she pulled a napkin over. You were the only tester at that shop who ever asked me what a test was for, she said. That's why you're here. That's the whole job.

Systems engineering is a way of making sure a whole thing works, for the people who need it, across its whole life. A system is a set of parts that interact to do something none of them can do alone. That last part is the point. A habitat module is a pressure shell, an air system, a thermal loop, power, data, crew quarters, and a hatch. None of those keeps four people alive. Together they might. The behavior that only shows up when the parts work together is called emergent behavior, and it's where both the value and the surprises live. Systems thinking means looking at the whole, the interactions, and the environment the system lives in, instead of one part at a time.

INCOSE's own definition says it in more formal words. Systems engineering is an approach that cuts across the engineering disciplines and ties them together, so that engineered systems get built, used and retired successfully. It draws on systems ideas and on scientific, technical and management methods. The words to hold onto are the whole, the people, and the life.

Why spend the effort? Because the early choices decide most of the cost. By the end of the concept stage, a program has spent only a small share of its money. But the decisions made by then lock in most of what the system will cost over its whole life: its size, its materials, how hard it is to build, how many people it takes to run and fix. A mistake caught on paper costs an eraser. The same mistake caught in test costs a redesign. Caught in orbit, it can cost the mission. Studies the handbook cites found that programs that put real effort into systems engineering early tended to overrun cost and schedule less, up to a point where more effort stopped paying back.

Systems nest inside each other. HEARTH is made of system elements, such as the air rack, and the air rack is a system in its own right, made of fans, sorbent beds, valves and a controller. Which one is the system of interest depends on whose job it is. For FRO it's HEARTH. If FRO buys the rack, the company that builds it has the rack as its system of interest. The processes in this book work at every level. Running them again on the level below is called recursion: requirements, architecture and verification for the module, then the same for the rack, then for the controller card. Running a process again at the same level, because something learned later changed the answer, is iteration. The handbook expects both. A program that never goes back to an earlier answer probably isn't learning anything.
Wes is right that he knows how to build a can, Colleen said. Your job is to make sure it's the right can.

How the exam asks it. Expect definition questions. When the question asks for a specific process, output or definition, answer that, even if another choice sounds broader. Only between choices that both fit the question does the one about the whole, the interactions, the stakeholders and the full life cycle usually win over one that optimizes a part in isolation. Early decisions commit most of the life cycle cost, which is why the effort goes in early. Recursion goes down a level. Iteration goes around again at the same level.

Nadia asked if there was a list for all of it, one page she could tape over her desk. Colleen laughed and turned the napkin over. There's a list, she said. It won't tell you what to do on Tuesday. It tells you what you'll be sorry about on Friday.

The first part of the handbook sets out a set of systems engineering principles, the ideas under every process in this course. In plain words, here are the ones the exam leans on. The work is fitted to the job: these stakeholders, this problem, this setting, so no two programs run it quite the same way. It looks at the whole: the parts, how they act on each other, the systems that support them, and the world around them. Stakeholder needs change, so the work keeps going back to the stakeholders for the whole life of the system, not just at the start. Decisions get made before all the facts are in, so every decision carries risk, and the risk gets weighed out loud. The job runs from the first idea to disposal. And complex systems get built by complex organizations, so a big share of the work is getting teams and disciplines to fit together, the same way the parts have to.

The handbook's full list runs longer, and a few more are worth knowing by name. Systems engineering is shaped by forces outside engineering: money, politics, the economy, society, technology, the environment and the law. Policy and law have to be understood well enough that the design is held to what they really say, no tighter and no looser. Once a real system exists, it's the only perfect model of itself, so every other model is an approximation with limits. The work builds a deeper understanding over time of how the system behaves, what it's sensitive to, and what its stakeholders need. It balances the technical need against budget and schedule instead of winning one by losing the others. A decision is only as good as what the people making it know about the system and the systems around it. Systems engineering pulls the disciplines into one effort, and it owns the interactions between them. And it rests on theory that's still being built, borrowed from systems science, engineering and management.

Two more ideas from that part of the handbook run all through this book. Uncertainty is normal. Early numbers are guesses, and good engineering says how good each guess is. Bias is normal too. People favor the answer they already like: the design they drew, the plan they wrote, the test that passed. Knowing that about yourself is part of the discipline.
Every pilot I ever flew with wanted the gauge to agree with them, Colleen said. The good ones checked it anyway. Nadia wrote that one on the napkin herself.

How the exam asks it. Principle questions usually reward the whole system, the whole life cycle and every stakeholder over one part, one stage or one team. A broad answer still loses to the precise process or term a question asks for. An answer that runs every program the same way, or waits for all the uncertainty to go away, is usually wrong. So is a design that reads a rule as stricter than it is and carries weight the rule never asked for.
The life cycle and its gates.

Colleen drew six boxes on the napkin. Every system moves through life cycle stages. The handbook's generic set is Concept, Development, Production, Utilization, Support, and Retirement. Concept is where you figure out what's needed and whether it's feasible. Development is where you define, design, build, verify, and validate it. Production makes it, Utilization is when people use it, Support keeps it working, and Retirement takes it out of service and disposes of it. Utilization and Support run side by side. HEARTH will spend fifteen years in those two stages, and somebody will eventually have to plan how it leaves orbit with the station.

Between stages sit decision gates. A gate is a planned point where leaders look at the evidence and decide what happens next. The options aren't just yes or no. They can proceed to the next stage, proceed with action items to close, keep working in the current one, go back to an earlier stage, put the project on hold, or end it. Technical reviews, like a system requirements review or a preliminary design review, feed those decisions with evidence.

The set of stages and gates a project actually runs is its life cycle model. Organizations keep standard ones, with what each stage is for, the gate criteria, and the reviews that feed each gate. That way projects don't each invent their own, and leaders can compare one project with another. Keeping those models current is an organizational process, life cycle model management, and you'll meet it properly at the end of the book. FRO's binder is a model like that, written for cargo. A project tailors the standard model to its own job, and writes down what it changed and why.

Each stage has its own question for the gate at its end. Concept asks whether there's a real need and a feasible way to meet it. Development asks whether the design meets its requirements and can be built and supported. Production asks whether units are coming out right, again and again. Utilization and Support ask whether the system is still doing its job, and at what cost. Retirement asks whether the way out is safe and complete.
Colleen put her fork down and tapped the napkin. A gate is where you're allowed to say we're not ready, she said. Use it.
How the exam asks it. Know the six generic stages in order, and know that Utilization and Support overlap. Know that a gate decision can be more than proceed or stop.

Then she drew a V. Down the left side you define: stakeholder needs, system requirements, architecture, design. At the bottom you build. Up the right side you integrate and prove: parts into subsystems, subsystems into the system, verifying each level against its own requirements as you go, and validating the whole against the stakeholders' needs at the top. Every level on the left has a partner on the right. The requirement you write on the way down is the thing you test on the way up.

The V shows two more things. Going down the left side is decomposition: each level splits the system into the elements below it and defines them. Going up the right side is integration and verification, one level at a time. And the V only loosely reads left to right as time. Real programs climb up and down it many times, which is the recursion and iteration from earlier.
She turned the napkin around so it faced Nadia. A test answers whatever question somebody wrote down, she said. Your job is making sure somebody wrote down the crew's.

The handbook organizes the work into four process groups from ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288. Agreement processes cover buying and supplying. Organizational project-enabling processes give projects what they need: life cycle models, infrastructure, portfolios, people, quality, and knowledge. Technical management processes plan, assess, decide, and control. Technical processes do the engineering, from mission analysis all the way to disposal. Verification asks whether you built it right, against the requirements. Validation asks whether you built the right thing, for the stakeholders, in the real environment.
How the exam asks it. Verification and validation questions are everywhere on this exam. Requirements go with verification. Stakeholder needs and intended use go with validation.
Mission analysis comes before the layout.

The first technical process is business or mission analysis. You ask why the system should exist, who it serves, what success looks like, and what constraints you can't move. You produce a problem statement and early life cycle concepts, including how it will be operated, before anyone draws a layout. For HEARTH that means asking what Halo is really trying to do with this module, not just what the contract volume is.

Here's the card for business or mission analysis. Its purpose is to define the problem or opportunity, describe the space a solution could live in, and name the classes of solution worth studying. It takes in the organization's goals and strategy, the problem as somebody first described it, the people with a stake, and the constraints nobody can move. It puts out a problem or opportunity statement, the solution classes to study, early measures of success, the business or mission requirements, and the first life cycle concepts, such as a preliminary operational concept built on the organization's concept of operations. Stakeholder needs and requirements definition picks those up next.

Mission analysis also asks whether a new system is the answer at all. Sometimes a change in procedure, in training, or to a system that already exists solves the problem for less, and those options get weighed beside the ones that build something new. Halo has already decided it wants a module. Even so, the question shapes what the module has to do.

Planning starts in the first week too. Project planning produces the plans, and for the engineering work that's usually a systems engineering management plan, or SEMP. It says which processes you'll use, how you'll tailor them, what reviews you'll hold, who owns what, and how technical work ties to the schedule. A work breakdown structure, or WBS, splits the whole job into pieces small enough to own, estimate and schedule, and the schedule, budget and staffing get built on those pieces.

Here's the card for project planning. Its purpose is to produce plans that will work and keep them current. It takes in the agreement, the project's goals and limits, the organization's standard processes and life cycle model, and the people, money and facilities on hand. It puts out the project's definition, with its objectives, scope, constraints and deliverables, plus the SEMP and other plans, the WBS, the schedule, budget and staffing built on it, and the roles that say who owns what. Project assessment and control uses those plans next, as the baseline it measures progress against. Every other process works inside them.

Planning doesn't end in week one. Plans get updated when scope changes, when a review moves, or when assessment shows the old plan no longer fits, and the updated plan becomes the new baseline. Estimates are strongest when they come from data on similar past work, adjusted for what's different this time. Two plans that disagree, a review in March in one and in May in the other, get reconciled before anyone works to either. And a plan that names tasks but not the test cell, the equipment and the people those tasks need isn't finished yet.
Wes wants a layout by Friday, Colleen said, finishing the pie. Give him something better by Friday. Give him the problem.

How the exam asks it. If a question describes a team jumping to a design before the problem is defined, the best answer goes back to mission analysis and stakeholder needs. Mission analysis hands a problem statement, solution classes and early concepts to stakeholder needs definition. Planning hands the SEMP, WBS and schedule to assessment and control.
Decision one. A layout by Friday.

Back from the diner, she found Wes already at the whiteboard with a marker. He drew a long cylinder, a hatch on one end, and started sketching four boxes along one wall. Crew quarters here. Galley in the middle. Hygiene on the far end so it's away from the food. Test kid, you can start tracking the mass.
It took her a second to realize the test kid was her. Jun glanced at her. Tiago raised an eyebrow over his coffee. What does Nadia do?
A. Start a mass tracker on Wes's layout and keep it current all week.
B. Let Wes keep sketching and draft a list of open questions on the side.
C. Tell Wes in front of the team that the layout is coming too early.
D. Ask Wes for two days to write up Halo's mission and constraints.

Nadia asks Wes for two days to write down what Halo is actually trying to do, before the boxes go on the board. Wes grunts. Two days. Nadia reads Halo's business plan, the station design guide, and the mission profile, and puts one page on his desk Wednesday night: what Halo is trying to do, how a crew will use the module, and the constraints nobody can move. Wes reads it twice and doesn't say anything. He also doesn't erase it.

That's the one. Business or mission analysis defines the problem and the solution space before anyone commits to a solution. It's quick when you do it early and very expensive when you skip it. You didn't fight Wes. You gave him a better starting line.
Tuesday morning Amara put the program schedule on the screen. It started with contract award and went straight to a preliminary design review in month four.
The contract's signed, so we're past the concept stuff, she said. We don't need a mission concept review or a requirements review. Halo already bought the module. I want to save the six weeks.
Amara's schedule runs from contract award straight to PDR in month four. What should Nadia propose?
A. Agree to drop both reviews and win back the six weeks for design.
B. Hold both reviews at full scale from the old government handbook.
C. Ask Halo's program office whether FRO should hold the early reviews.
D. Fold the two reviews into one short gate sized to HEARTH's risk.

Nadia proposes folding the two reviews into one short gate sized to HEARTH's risk. Amara pushes back, then agrees to a combined review in week six, one day long, with clear entry and exit criteria. It costs her two weeks instead of six, and she gets a written baseline she can hold Halo to.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Life cycle stages end in decision gates, and a gate only works if somebody's willing to say not yet. Tailoring means right sizing the review, not deleting it. You kept the decision and cut the overhead.
Amara stopped by Nadia's desk after lunch. I have a schedule. I don't have an engineering plan. Halo's contract asks for one in thirty days. What do you need from me?
Nadia had written test plans. She had never written a plan for how an entire program does its engineering.
Halo's contract asks for an engineering plan in thirty days. What should Nadia produce?
A. Add an engineering column with owners and review dates to Amara's schedule.
B. Draft a SEMP from the handbook outline, with each tailoring choice explained.
C. Rename FRO's last cargo module SEMP for HEARTH and send it to Halo on time.
D. Write the SEMP once the first design review has settled the baseline.

She drafts a systems engineering management plan, a SEMP, from the handbook outline, borrowing what still fits from the cargo one and marking every tailoring choice with a reason. Amara reads the review section, adds two milestones to her schedule, and says, Now I can defend this.

Exactly right. Project planning produces the plans that tell everyone how the technical work will happen. The SEMP is the engineering half of that. Writing tailoring decisions down, with reasons, is what separates tailoring from skipping.
FRO had a binder. Literally a binder, three inches thick, called the Product Development Process. Wes had written most of it ten years ago for cargo modules. Every program at FRO followed it.

Reading it Wednesday night, Nadia found what she half expected. There was no step for a crew safety review, no human factors evaluation, nothing about a hazard report. The binder had been built for modules that carried food and spare parts.
Every FRO program follows the Product Development Process binder. What should Nadia do for HEARTH?
A. Run HEARTH from the INCOSE handbook directly and set the binder aside.
B. Take the gap to the binder's owner with a proposed crewed tailoring.
C. Write the missing crew safety steps into her personal checklist.
D. Follow the binder as written and log the missing crew steps as a risk.

She takes the gap to whoever owns the binder, with two pages of crewed steps. The owner turns out to be Wes. He reads them, grumbles about the length, and signs it. Should have done this when we bid it. The binder gets a new tab: crewed programs.

That's the one. Life cycle model management means the organization owns its processes and improves them deliberately. When a new kind of program shows up, you change the model through its owner. Next time the steps are already there.
Decision five. Who cares about this module.
Jun had started a stakeholder list in the model. It had two names on it: Halo Orbital and FRO.
That's who signed the contract, he said. Who else is there?
Jun's model lists two stakeholders, Halo Orbital and FRO. How should Nadia shape the list?
A. Widen the list to everyone HEARTH touches, from launch to disposal.
B. Add the astronauts as the real users and leave the rest to Amara's team.
C. Ask Halo for its own stakeholder list and adopt it for HEARTH.
D. Keep the two contract parties for now and add others as they come up.

Nadia widens it to everyone HEARTH touches, from launch to disposal. The list grows to fourteen. Jun adds a column for what each one needs and another for how they'd know the module works. Two of the fourteen, the station's robotic arm team and the disposal planners, have requirements nobody had heard of.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Stakeholder identification covers the whole life cycle: users, operators, maintainers, regulators, interfacing systems, and the people who'll retire it. Each brings needs, and missing needs become missing requirements.

Thursday, reading the statement of work line by line, Nadia found a sentence that bothered her. "Habitable volume shall be at least 90 cubic meters." There was no definition of habitable volume anywhere in the contract.
Pressurized volume, the inside of the shell, was about ninety. Habitable volume, the space a person can actually move in after the racks and quarters are installed, would be a lot less.
Nobody has said what habitable volume means in this contract. What should Nadia do?
A. Grow the module until it meets either reading of habitable volume.
B. Call Helen at Halo and design to the definition she gives.
C. Design to the pressurized volume HEARTH already meets.
D. Ask Amara to send Halo a formal request to define the term.

Amara sends a formal clarification request through the contracts channel that afternoon. Halo's answer comes back in a week, in writing, and it's the habitable reading. Nadia is glad she asked in week one instead of month nine.

Exactly right. In the supply process, the supplier makes sure it understands what the acquirer is asking for and that the agreement says it clearly. Ambiguity gets resolved through the agreement, in writing, early.

By Thursday afternoon Nadia had found three versions of the HEARTH mission profile. One was on Wes's laptop, one was attached to an email chain, and one was printed and pinned to the wall in the high bay with handwritten notes.
They disagreed about how long the crew stays. Ninety days on Wes's laptop. A hundred and eighty on the wall, in somebody's handwriting.
Nadia has found three copies of the mission profile in three places. What's the right fix?
A. Name Wes's laptop copy the master and tell the team to use it.
B. Send everyone the newest version, and ask them to delete the rest.
C. Set up one controlled repository with an owner for each document.
D. Keep a page in her notebook tracking which version is current.

Nadia sets up one controlled repository and gives every document an owner. It takes a day of setup and a short note to the team. Tiago is the first to move his test documents in. The pinned printout in the high bay gets a sticky note on it: "Current version lives here," with a link.

That's the one. Information management makes sure the right people have the right information, current and controlled, for the whole life cycle. On a fifteen year program, where things live is an engineering decision.
Decision eight. Saying it to Wes.

By Thursday evening the pattern was clear. Wes made calls fast, and his calls were usually right, and nobody ever asked him why. Nadia had three things she needed to raise with him: the layout, the binder, and the volume question.
She was thirty one. He'd been building pressure vessels since before she was born. Her stomach did the thing it always did before she told somebody senior they might be wrong.
The layout, the binder and the volume question all need to reach Wes. How should Nadia raise them?
A. Ask Wes for twenty minutes alone and hear his view on each first.
B. Wait a few months, build some credibility, then raise all three.
C. Bring the three issues to Amara and let her decide what goes to Wes.
D. Lay out all three issues in an email to Wes with Amara copied.

She asks Wes for twenty minutes alone and asks for his view on each thing before she gives hers. Wes talks for fifteen of the twenty minutes, about a cargo module in 2019 that leaked at the hatch seal and how he found it. Then he listens. On the volume question he says, Good catch. On the layout he says, Fine. Give me your problem statement. But I'm not waiting forever.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Systems engineering is a team sport, and influence is part of the job. Go to the person first, privately, with curiosity before conclusions. You learned something from him, and he heard you because you asked first.
Decision nine. The test engineer's instinct.

Tiago pulled up a chair Friday morning. You're a test person. I'm a test person. Let's get ahead of it. Help me start the verification plan now and we'll be the only program at FRO that isn't scrambling at the end.
It was exactly what Nadia was good at, and she felt the pull. She also knew what she was reaching for: the moment a test came back green and everybody got to go home.
Tiago asks Nadia to help him start test planning now. What should she do?
A. Start drafting the verification plan with Tiago this week.
B. Work with Tiago on how Halo will decide HEARTH works for a crew.
C. Ask Tiago to hold test planning until the design is done at CDR.
D. Ask Halo to define the acceptance tests HEARTH will have to pass.

Nadia asks him to start one level up, with how Halo will decide HEARTH works for a crew. Tiago thinks about it and grins. Validation first. I like it. They draft four questions for Halo about how a crew will actually live in and leave the module, and the first one is about a fire.

Exactly right. Validation asks whether you built the right thing for its intended use. Setting validation intent early means the requirements, and then the verification, point at what the crew actually needs.
Amara needed a drafter for Wes's layout drawings and had Jun's name on a sticky note.

Jun had told Nadia on Tuesday that he'd joined FRO to do model-based systems engineering, and that this was the first program where anyone had let him open the modeling tool. He had a SysML model of the stakeholder list already. He'd built it on his own time.
Amara has Jun's name down to draft Wes's layout drawings. What should Nadia do?
A. Encourage Jun to make his own case to Amara for the model work.
B. Split Jun's week between Wes's drawings and the system model.
C. Make the case to Amara for putting Jun on the system model.
D. Let Amara put Jun on drafting for the first quarter of the program.

Nadia makes the case for putting Jun on the system model instead. Amara agrees, on the condition Nadia finds her a drafter. Nadia does, a contractor Tiago knows. Jun gets the model and a development plan with two milestones on it. He brings Nadia a coffee the next morning without saying why.
That's the one. Projects need the right people with the right competencies, and people need to grow. You matched the skill to the work, solved the manager's real problem, and invested in someone.
At Friday's staff meeting Nadia suggested inviting someone from FRO's tiny safety office and a human factors specialist to the concept work.
Safety reviews the design, test kid, Wes said. They don't make it. They'll get it at PDR like always.
When should FRO's safety office first get involved in HEARTH?
A. Bring safety and human factors into the concept work starting this week.
B. Write the first hazard list herself and bring the specialists in at PDR.
C. Leave the first safety review at PDR where FRO's binder puts it.
D. Have safety review the concept once it's written, well ahead of PDR.

Nadia doesn't let it go, and safety and human factors join the concept work that week. The safety engineer is a quiet woman named Odette. In the first meeting she asks one question, where the crew goes if the air goes bad, and nobody has an answer. Now it's on the list.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Quality characteristics, like safety and human systems integration, get designed in. On a crewed program they belong in the concept, because the cheapest time to remove a hazard is before anyone has drawn it.
Friday at four, Halo's director of crew operations called in for a get-to-know-you. Helen Cho-Ramirez had spent eleven years as a flight surgeon for long duration crews, and she didn't waste time.

I read your contract. It says ninety cubic meters. That's not what I need. I need four people to live in there for six months, and if there's a fire in the galley at three in the morning, I need all four of them to get out, or to a safe place, before the smoke gets them. I don't see that anywhere in the paperwork.
This was supposed to be a get to know you call. What should Nadia do with what Helen said?
A. Tell Helen the need isn't in the contract and would take a change order.
B. Promise Helen a safe haven and two egress paths in the design.
C. Write the need down in Helen's words and ask her to walk through it.
D. Ask Helen to send the need in writing through Halo's program office.

Nadia asks three follow up questions: how long smoke takes to become dangerous, where Helen thinks the crew sleeps, and what the old station did. Helen answers all three in detail. At the end she says, Call me after you've timed it.

Exactly right. A stakeholder need, stated in the stakeholder's words, is gold. Capture it, understand it, and take it into needs and requirements definition, where it can be traced and, if needed, handled through the agreement. Don't dismiss it and don't promise around it.

Nadia stayed late Friday. She opened a new document in the repository she had set up on Thursday, titled it HEARTH Stakeholder Needs, and typed Helen's words exactly as Helen had said them, three in the morning and all.

It had been a good week, and she knew it. She'd given Wes a problem instead of a fight, kept the gates without wasting the schedule, and gotten the volume question in writing before anyone built to the wrong number. On his way out Wes stopped at her desk. Night, Brooks. She was halfway to the car before she noticed.
On the drive home she called her father. Frank Brooks picked up on the first ring, the way he always did.
So, he said. They figure out what they hired yet?

I think I found a question nobody's asked, she said. She told him about Helen, about the galley fire at three in the morning, about four people in a can two hundred and fifty miles up with nowhere to go.
He was quiet for a while. He went quiet like that whenever work got anywhere close to the year he stopped climbing.
Then that's your job, he said. Somebody's got to be the one who asks where they go.
Then his voice changed, the way it did when he got to the part he'd been saving. Rosie wants to know if you live in space now. I told her not yet.
Nadia laughed, and it caught a little on the way out. She told him she'd come down soon. Okay, he said. He'd heard that one before. He said okay anyway.
Monday morning Helen's email was waiting.

An email from Helen Cho-Ramirez. Subject: Following up on fire and safe haven. Nadia, Thank you for Friday. I've attached the old station's emergency response times for fire and depressurization, and a sketch of where I think the crew sleeps. On the old station we timed it once: bunk to hatch, lights out, alarm going. Nobody has timed yours. I want that number before anybody draws a wall. Helen
